::: {.lead}
*Pocket Quest 1.1* gets an online mode: two players race on the same
island, and a leaderboard shows the best times. Now every match depends on
the **network**: Rami's test phone must send its position to the game
server many times per second, and a purchase of gems must never get lost.
Byte Bay also moves into a new office and needs a network for its PCs and
test phones. In this lesson you learn what a network is made of, how
devices find each other with addresses and names, how data travels in
packets with protocols, and which network quality a game needs. Every
section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary computer-network lan wan internet router network-switch access-point ip-address mac-address dns network-packet network-protocol tcp udp network-latency >}}

## 19.1 Networks: from the LAN to the Internet

A **network** connects devices so that they can exchange data. The office
of Byte Bay has a small network of its own, and through it, the whole
Internet (@fig-lan).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 19.1 — LAN, WAN, Internet and their devices"}
- A **LAN** (local area network) covers one place: an office, a lab, a
  home. A **WAN** connects places far apart. The **Internet** is the
  worldwide network of networks.
- A **switch** connects the wired devices of a LAN.
- A **wireless access point** connects Wi-Fi devices to the LAN.
- A **router** connects the LAN to other networks; through the **ISP**
  (Internet service provider) it reaches the Internet. At home, one box is
  often router, switch, access point and modem together.
:::

![The network of Byte Bay.](images/lan-map.png){#fig-lan width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 19.1 — The new office"}
1. Four PCs and the printer are cabled to a **switch**.
2. An **access point** on the switch gives Wi-Fi to the test phones P5 and
   P8.
3. A **router** connects the switch to the ISP and the Internet, where the
   game server *play.example.net* runs.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"The Wi-Fi is the Internet." Wi-Fi only connects the phone to the access
point in the same room. Behind it are the LAN, the router, the ISP and
many networks.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your network"}
Draw the network at your home or in your lab: the devices, the box (or
boxes) that act as router and access point, and the way to the Internet.

*Your result:* a drawing with at least five labelled parts.
:::

## 19.2 Addresses: IP, MAC and the DNS

A packet needs an address, like a letter. Networks use numbers, and the
DNS turns names into numbers (@fig-addr).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 19.2 — IP address, MAC address, DNS"}
- An **IP address** identifies a device on a network, such as
  192.168.1.23 (IPv4: four numbers from 0 to 255). Addresses that start
  with 192.168, 10 or 172.16–31 are **private**: they work only inside a
  LAN. The router has a **public** address on the Internet. IPv6 uses
  longer addresses.
- A **MAC address** is the fixed address of a network card, used inside one
  LAN.
- The **DNS** (Domain Name System) turns a name such as play.example.net
  into an IP address.
:::

![IP and MAC addresses, and a DNS question.](images/addresses.png){#fig-addr width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 19.2 — The phone finds the server"}
1. The game knows only the name *play.example.net*.
2. The phone asks the DNS server: the answer is **198.51.100.7**.
3. The phone sends its packets to 198.51.100.7, through its **default
   gateway**, the router 192.168.1.1.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Writing a private address such as 192.168.1.23 in the game as the server
address. Players outside the office cannot reach it. A server on the
Internet needs a public address, and the game should use its name.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Find your address"}
On a phone: Settings › Wi-Fi › the network › details. On a PC: run
`ipconfig` (Windows) or `ip a` (Linux). Write your IP address and your
gateway. Is the address private?

*Your result:* two addresses and one answer.
:::

## 19.3 Packets and protocols

Data does not travel as one big piece. It is cut into **packets**, and
every device on the way follows the same **protocols** (@fig-layers).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 19.3 — Packets and protocols in four layers"}
A **packet** is a small piece of data with the addresses of the sender and
the receiver. A **protocol** is a set of rules for exchanging data. The
**TCP/IP model** has four layers:

1. **Application:** what the app wants to say (HTTPS for web services, DNS
   for names, the game's own messages).
2. **Transport:** TCP or UDP, with a port number for the app.
3. **Internet:** IP addresses; routers forward each packet.
4. **Link:** the next step on a cable (Ethernet) or by radio (Wi-Fi).
:::

![The four layers.](images/layers.png){#fig-layers width=94%}

The two transport protocols suit different game data (@fig-tcpudp).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 19.4 — TCP and UDP"}
**TCP** checks that every packet arrives, in order, and sends lost
packets again: it is reliable but can wait. **UDP** sends packets without
checking: it is fast, and lost packets stay lost.
:::

![TCP and UDP with one lost packet.](images/tcp-udp.png){#fig-tcpudp width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 19.3 — Two kinds of data in Pocket Quest"}
1. **Positions** in a race: 30 per second over **UDP**. If one is lost, the
   next one is newer anyway; waiting would make the game lag.
2. **A purchase** of 100 gems: over **HTTPS**, which uses TCP. Every byte
   must arrive, and nobody may read or change it.
3. The leaderboard and the save game also use HTTPS over TCP.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/packet-journey.html" poster="sims/packet-journey.png" title="Packet Journey: TCP or UDP?" height="720" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"UDP is bad because it loses packets." For live positions and voice, UDP
is the right choice: a late packet is worse than a lost one.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · TCP or UDP?"}
1. In **Packet Journey**, send 10 packets with TCP and with UDP, both with
   20 % loss. Compare the missing packets and the time.
2. Choose TCP or UDP for: a chat message, voice chat, a download of a new
   level.

*Your result:* two results and three choices.
:::

## 19.4 Network quality for games

A fast connection for videos is not always good for games. Games need low
and steady delays (@fig-quality).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 19.5 — Latency, jitter, packet loss, bandwidth"}
- **Latency** (ping): the time a packet needs to go and come back, in
  milliseconds.
- **Jitter:** how much the latency changes from packet to packet.
- **Packet loss:** the share of packets that never arrive.
- **Bandwidth:** the amount of data per second, in Mbit/s.

An action game needs low latency, low jitter and almost no loss; it needs
little bandwidth.
:::

![Network quality for an online game.](images/net-quality.png){#fig-quality width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 19.4 — Rami tests the race"}
1. At his desk, on cable: ping 22 ms, no loss. The race runs smoothly.
2. On Wi-Fi, two rooms away: ping 30–180 ms, 5 % loss. The other car jumps
   on the screen.
3. On 4G in the bus: ping 60 ms, steady. The race is playable, with a small
   delay.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Buying more bandwidth to fix lag. 100 Mbit/s does not help when the Wi-Fi
signal is weak and packets get lost.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Compare"}
Play an online game (or open a speed test) twice: on Wi-Fi near the router,
then far from it or on mobile data. Write the ping both times.

*Your result:* two ping values and one sentence.
:::

## Case study: Net Fixer

Byte Bay moves into a new office and Rami sets up the network for testing:
the PCs need a device that joins their cables, the test phones need Wi-Fi,
the LAN needs a way to the Internet, the phone must find
*play.example.net*, a PC needs an address, and the game must send
positions and purchases with the right protocol. The Game challenge of the
interactive lesson uses this office. In the mini-game below you choose the
right device, address or protocol for each job.

## Further reading

Kurose and Ross, *Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach*, 8th ed.,
Chapter 1 (the Internet, packets, delay and loss) and Sections 2.4 (DNS)
and 3.3 (UDP). Glazer and Madhav, *Multiplayer Game Programming* (2015),
Chapter 2.

## Exercises

1. What is the difference between a LAN and the Internet?
2. Which device connects the wired PCs of an office?
3. Which device connects the LAN to the ISP?
4. Is 192.168.0.15 a private or a public address?
5. What does the DNS do?
6. What is a packet?
7. Name the four layers of the TCP/IP model.
8. Why do games send live positions over UDP?
9. Which protocol does a purchase use?
10. A player has 200 Mbit/s but 8 % packet loss. Is the game smooth?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. A LAN covers one place; the Internet is the worldwide network of
   networks.
2. A switch.
3. A router.
4. Private.
5. It turns a name such as play.example.net into an IP address.
6. A small piece of data with the addresses of the sender and the
   receiver.
7. Application, transport, Internet, link.
8. They are fast, and a lost position is replaced by the next one.
9. HTTPS over TCP.
10. No: the lost packets make players jump, whatever the bandwidth.
:::
